#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Census of Agriculture
Description: The Census of Agriculture, conducted once every five years, looks at land use and ownership, producer characteristics, production practices, income, and expenditures. The Census of Agriculture is a complete count of U.S. farms and ranches and the people who operate them. Even small plots of land - whether rural or urban - count if $1,000 or more of agricultural products were produced and sold, or normally would have been sold, during the census year.
URL: https://nass.usda.gov/AgCensus

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Census of Agriculture
Description: The Census of Agriculture, conducted once every five years, looks at land use and ownership, producer characteristics, production practices, income, and expenditures. The Census of Agriculture is a complete count of U.S. farms and ranches and the people who operate them. Even small plots of land - whether rural or urban - count if $1,000 or more of agricultural products were produced and sold, or normally would have been sold, during the census year.
URL: https://nass.usda.gov/AgCensus

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Census of Agriculture comprehensively. Let me start with several searches.Good start. Let me dig deeper into the 2022 census details, methodology, confidentiality protections, and data users.Now let me research data users, special products, historical archives, and upcoming census plans.The Wikipedia page returned mostly boilerplate. Let me fetch the official 2022 Census introduction document, which covers history, authority, uses, and methodology.I have substantial material. Let me try one more search to round out historical archives and future plans.I've reached the search limit, but I've gathered comprehensive, well-sourced information. Here is the full report.

---

# Research Report: The Census of Agriculture

## 1. Verification of Your Description

Your information is **accurate**, with a few nuances worth noting:

- ✅ **Title and URL**: Correct — "Census of Agriculture," published at https://nass.usda.gov/AgCensus.
- ✅ **Frequency**: Conducted every five years, in years ending in "2" and "7" (data reference year; collection and publication follow).
- ✅ **Farm definition**: Correct — any place (rural *or* urban) from which $1,000 or more of agricultural products were produced and sold, or normally would have been sold, during the census year. This $1,000 threshold has been in effect since the 1974 census (definitions varied in earlier censuses, which matters for historical comparability).
- ✅ **Content**: Land use and ownership, producer characteristics, production practices, income, and expenditures — all confirmed.
- ⚠️ **Nuance on "complete count"**: While the census *aims* for a complete count, the published figures are not raw tallies. Because of declining response rates, NASS publishes estimates statistically adjusted for undercoverage, nonresponse, and misclassification using capture-recapture methodology (details below). This is important for data scientists interpreting the numbers.

---

## 2. Publisher and Legal Authority

**Publisher**: The U.S. Department of Agriculture's **National Agricultural Statistics Service (USDA NASS)**, the principal federal statistical agency for agriculture. Contact: USDA-NASS, 1400 Independence Ave. SW, Washington, DC 20250; data inquiries (800) 727-9540.

**Statutory mandate**: The **Census of Agriculture Act of 1997** (Public Law 105-113, enacted November 21, 1997), codified at **7 U.S.C. § 2204g**. Key provisions:

- The Secretary of Agriculture *shall* take a census of agriculture in 1998 and every fifth year thereafter, covering the year immediately preceding the census year.
- The Secretary may use any survey, sampling, or statistical method deemed appropriate.
- **Response is mandatory by law**: willfully giving a false answer carries a fine up to $500; refusing or willfully neglecting to answer carries a fine up to $100. (No one can be compelled to disclose their Social Security number or religious affiliation.)
- Geographic coverage must include all 50 states, and as the Secretary determines, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and American Samoa (all of which are currently covered).

**Confidentiality authority**: Respondent data are protected by **7 U.S.C. § 2276** and the **Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (CIPSEA) of 2018** (Title III of P.L. 115-435, 44 U.S.C. Ch. 35). Individual responses are used for statistical purposes only, are **immune from FOIA requests and legal subpoena**, and cannot be used for regulatory, tax, or law-enforcement purposes. Willful unauthorized disclosure is a Class E felony — up to $250,000 in fines and five years in prison. NASS suppresses published cells (e.g., combining counties) where a single operation could be identified.

---

## 3. History

The Census of Agriculture is one of the oldest federal statistical programs:

- **1810**: A single question on engagement in agriculture appeared in the decennial census (~80% of Americans were so engaged).
- **1840**: First dedicated agricultural census, part of the decennial census; the value of the data led to permanent expansion of the census program.
- **1850–1920**: Agriculture census conducted decennially by what became the U.S. Census Bureau (Department of Commerce).
- **1915**: Congress authorized quinquennial (5-year) collection; implemented with the **1925** mid-decade census.
- **By 1950**: To spread the Census Bureau's workload, the agriculture census shifted to years ending in "4" and "9" while economic censuses used "2" and "7."
- **1976 (P.L. 94-229)**: Shortened the interval after the 1974 census to realign agriculture with the economic censuses for years ending in "2" and "7," beginning 1982.
- **1997 (P.L. 105-113)**: Responsibility transferred from the Census Bureau to USDA NASS. The **1997 Census of Agriculture** was the first conducted by NASS, which completed all collection, analysis, tabulation, and publication under Title 7 authority. (NASS still reimburses the Census Bureau for some island-area enumeration work.)

This 1997 transfer is significant for preservationists: it means pre-1997 censuses live in the Census Bureau's archival lineage (Title 13) and post-1997 censuses in USDA's (Title 7), with differing confidentiality regimes and archival homes.

---

## 4. The Most Recent Census (2022) and Key Findings

- **Timeline**: Questionnaires mailed November–December 2022 covering the 2022 calendar year; responses accepted (online or mail) through May 2023; full results released **February 13, 2024**, with follow-on products through late 2024/2025 (Web Maps September 2024; ZIP code tabulations November 2024; Puerto Rico and island-area reports into 2025).
- **Scale**: More than **6 million data points** down to the county level.
- **Response rate**: **61.0%** — down sharply from 71.8% (2017) and 74.6% (2012); over 40% of responses came in online. This decline is a major data-quality story and the reason statistical adjustment matters so much.
- **Headline findings**:
  - **1,900,487 farms**, down 6.9% from 2,042,220 in 2017 — continuing long-term consolidation.
  - **880.1 million acres** in farms (~39% of all U.S. land), down 20.1 million acres.
  - **Average farm size**: 463 acres, up 5% from 441.
  - Growth in **new and beginning producers** (≤10 years farming) and **young producers** (under 35); the share of farms with more than one decision-maker rose from 54% to 60%.

---

## 5. Methodology (for data scientists)

- **Frame**: The Census Mail List (CML) — NASS's list of known and potential farm operations, maintained continuously from surveys and administrative sources (e.g., Farm Service Agency records).
- **Modes**: Primarily mail and internet (Computer-Assisted Self Interview), with CATI (telephone) and CAPI (in-person) follow-up by enumerators at NASS Data Collection Centers for nonresponse and special records. Paper returns are imaged and keyed from images.
- **Adjustment**: Published totals are **capture-recapture estimates**. The census (list-frame) and the June Area Survey (JAS, an independent area-frame survey) serve as two "captures"; models estimate the probability that a true farm was on the CML, responded, and was correctly classified as a farm. Weights correct for undercoverage, nonresponse, and misclassification. In 2022 the methodology was extended to a single capture-probability model using all census responses and JAS records (documented in Volume 1, Appendix A).
- **Editing/imputation**: Data are reviewed for consistency and completeness, with imputation for item nonresponse.
- **Geographic assignment**: Multi-county and multi-state operations are split so production is attributed to the correct county/state.

**Comparability cautions**: Farm definitions have changed over the decades; terminology shifted from "operator" to "producer" in 2017 (allowing up to four producers per farm and changing demographic series); and commodity classifications follow NAICS. NASS publishes crosswalks and flags breaks in series.

---

## 6. Data Products and Access

All products are free and public domain:

- **Volume 1, Geographic Area Series**: National-, state-, and county-level data — the core release (PDF, TXT, and by-table CSV). Puerto Rico and island areas (Guam, U.S. Virgin Islands, Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa) get separate reports.
- **Volume 2, Subject Series**: Cross-tabulations and special topics (e.g., history, rankings by market value).
- **Volume 3, Special Studies**: Follow-on studies.
- **Ag Census Highlights**: Topical fact sheets (farms and farmland, economics, producers, etc.).
- **Ag Census Web Maps**: Interactive mapping application.
- **ZIP Code Tabulations**: New for 2022 — farm counts and characteristics by five-digit ZIP code, with a published methodology.
- **Quick Stats 2.0** (quickstats.nass.usda.gov): The primary queryable database — custom queries by commodity, location (national/state/county/ZIP), and year; bulk downloads as .gz files updated daily; and a **public API** (see nass.usda.gov/developer). NASS provides a user guide crosswalking Volume 1 tables to Quick Stats metadata.
- **Census Data Query Tool (CDQT)**: Table-level access for the 2012 and 2017 censuses.
- **Restricted microdata**: Record-level data (2007 and newer) are accessible only to approved researchers via the **Special Sworn Agent** program — Standard Application Process (SAP), Data Access and Disclosure Review Board approval, secure data enclave, variable-level justification, and mandatory disclosure review of all outputs. Custom aggregations can also be commissioned as paid special tabulations.

**Archives for preservationists**:
- NASS hosts an online archive of census reports **2002 and earlier** at nass.usda.gov/AgCensus/archive.
- **Cornell University's Albert R. Mann Library** maintains a major digitized Census of Agriculture collection (agcensus.library.cornell.edu), including historical volumes, as part of the USDA Economics, Statistics, and Market Information System partnership with the National Agricultural Library.
- The **Census Bureau** (census.gov/library/publications/time-series/agriculture.html) retains the historical time series for the censuses it conducted (1840–1992).
- NASS reports are also distributed through the **Federal Depository Library Program** and govinfo.gov.

---

## 7. Users and Uses

Per NASS and the census's own documentation, routine users include:

- **Congress and state legislatures**: Shaping farm bills and farm/rural policy; evaluating historical trends to design programs.
- **Federal agencies**: The Farm Service Agency uses census data for county committee election representation (race/ethnicity/gender), beginning-farmer loan eligibility (county average farm size), and funding targets for socially disadvantaged producers; the Risk Management Agency uses NASS county data in federal crop insurance; NRCS and ERS analysts use it for conservation and economic research.
- **State and local governments / community planners**: Targeting services to rural residents; allocating extension, research, soil conservation, and land-grant university funds.
- **Agribusiness, cooperatives, and trade associations**: Siting facilities near production areas; market analysis; benchmarks for commodity sectors — including uncommon/specialty crops and livestock for which the census is often the *only* data source.
- **Farmers and ranchers**: Business planning and benchmarking their own operations against county/state averages.
- **Researchers, universities, and journalists**: The census is the only source of comparable county-level statistics classifying farms by size, tenure, organization type, producer demographics, sales class, and NAICS code.

**Public benefits**: NASS data are objective, timely, and equally available to all — reducing market uncertainty, leveling the playing field between large and small market participants, and underpinning billions of dollars in farm program payments, disaster assistance, and rural development allocations. The census is also the authoritative demographic record of American farmers — age, race, ethnicity, gender, and military service — central to equity policy debates (e.g., documenting the decline of Black farmland ownership and the rise of women producers).

---

## 8. Issues, Risks, and Things a Policy Activist or Preservationist Should Watch

1. **Declining response rates** (74.6% → 71.8% → 61.0% over three censuses) increase reliance on modeled adjustment and raise nonresponse-bias questions, even though NASS's capture-recapture methodology is well documented.
2. **Statutory fragility and funding**: The census exists only because P.L. 105-113 mandates it, but NASS has faced budget pressure — in August 2025 NASS announced discontinuation of several other data collection programs and reports. The census itself is the statutory anchor that protects much of the surrounding agricultural statistics infrastructure.
3. **No public microdata**: Because of CIPSEA and § 2276, there will never be a public-use microdata file like the Census Bureau's. Researchers depend on the sworn-agent enclave process; preservationists should ensure published aggregates (including suppressed-cell documentation) are archived, since they are the *only* public record.
4. **Series breaks**: Definition and terminology changes (farm definition, operator→producer in 2017, internet-access and renewable-energy questions added over time) complicate longitudinal analysis.
5. **Format longevity**: Current dissemination depends on Quick Stats and web applications; the durable preservation copies are the PDF/TXT/CSV Volume 1–3 publications and bulk Quick Stats files. The Cornell/NAL partnership is the key third-party preservation channel.
6. **Next edition**: The **2027 Census of Agriculture** (reference year 2027, mailing late 2027/early 2028, results expected 2029) is in preparation — a January 2025 Federal Register notice began the OMB information-collection revision process, which is the public's formal opportunity to comment on content changes.

---

## Key Sources

# Dataset Risk Assessment: Census of Agriculture (USDA NASS)

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- All products from the two most recent censuses (2017, 2022) remain available on nass.usda.gov/Publications/AgCensus, and historical census data back to 1997 remain queryable in Quick Stats 2.0 (including the 2022 ZIP-code tabulations added in November 2024).
- Historical reports (2002 and prior) remain accessible: the NASS archive URL now serves/mirrors the Cornell University Mann Library AgCensus digital collection (agcensus.library.cornell.edu), an independent third-party preservation home. The Census Bureau also retains its time series for the 1840–1992 censuses it conducted.
- No reports of removal or alteration of any prior-cycle census files.

**Evidence for higher levels:** None found. No data files or data elements from prior cycles are known to have been removed. (The hosting migration of the pre-2002 archive from NASS infrastructure to Cornell is a change in location, not a loss — and arguably improves preservation redundancy.)

**Finding: No Known Issue.** Prior-cycle data remain accessible without known alterations, and preservation is actually strengthened by the Cornell mirror.

---

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The census is statutorily required every five years (7 U.S.C. § 2204g), and the 2027 cycle is proceeding on the normal timeline: content-request notice (July 19, 2024, 89 FR 58716); 60-day PRA notice (Jan. 14, 2026, 91 FR 1501); 30-day notice (May 29, 2026, 91 FR 31996); **OIRA approved the ICR (0535-0226) with change on September 16, 2026**, active through September 30, 2029 — covering the entire collection and publication window (omb.report ICR 202605-0535-002).
- FY2026 appropriations agreement provides $185M for NASS, of which $46M is for the Census of Agriculture, and **explicitly directs NASS to continue all activities and reports at FY2023 frequency levels** (Senate Appropriations, Division B JES).
- The 2022 census was published on schedule (Feb. 13, 2024) with all follow-on products delivered.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The previous ICR approval expired 9/30/2024, leaving a ~2-year lapse before the 9/16/2026 reinstatement. However, this between-cycle lapse-and-reinstate pattern is standard for the quinquennial census (the 2022 cycle followed the same pattern) and has now been cured.
- Census-program staffing was cut from 230 FTE (FY2025) to 100 FTE (FY2026 budget) just ahead of the census year (USDA FY2026 Explanatory Notes) — a serious execution risk, though better captured under Staffing/Data Quality.

**Evidence for High Risk:** No missed statutory deadline; collection not skipped; ICR currently active.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** The statutory schedule is being met and the ICR is active through 2029. The staffing-driven execution risk is real but is scored in the categories below.

## Data Quality

**Evidence for High Risk (reductions in granularity/timeliness/frequency):**
- At the agency level, NASS has already cut products: the Agricultural Labor Survey and Mink Survey were discontinued (Aug. 2025; 90 FR 42560); state- and region-specific reports were eliminated (May 2025); the July Cattle report and county estimates were canceled in April 2024 before Congress forced reinstatement.
- However, **none of these cuts touch the Census of Agriculture itself**, which is congressionally protected at full frequency.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk (potential/emerging risk):**
- The FY2026 budget cuts **Census of Agriculture program staffing from 230 to 100 FTEs (-57%)** immediately before the 2027 census — an unmistakable emerging risk to the census's quality, field follow-up capacity, and timeliness.
- Agency-wide staffing loss (41–54%) is degrading methodological upkeep; the American Statistical Association rates NASS resources "WEAK" and warns its Evidence Act responsibilities are "severely challenged." ASA also cites a January 2026 corn-acreage revision episode that moved markets as evidence of quality strain.
- Secular decline in census response rates (74.6% → 71.8% → 61.0% over 2012–2022) increases reliance on statistical adjustment; lower field capacity in 2027 could worsen this.
- Positive counterweight: the 2022 census *added* granularity (first-ever ZIP code tabulations), and the FY2026 appropriations directive mandates FY2023-level frequency.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** Census granularity and schedule have, to date, been maintained or improved.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** The census product itself has not been degraded, but the halving of census-program staff on the eve of the 2027 cycle, agency-wide product terminations, and independent expert warnings constitute clear emerging risk to timeliness and quality.

## Statutory Context

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The census is **explicitly mandated**: the Census of Agriculture Act of 1997 (P.L. 105-113; 7 U.S.C. § 2204g) requires the Secretary of Agriculture to conduct it every five years, specifies coverage (50 states plus territories), and makes response mandatory. The OMB ICR itself cites § 2204g and describes the census as "the only source of consistent, comparable agricultural data at the county, state, and national levels" — i.e., **no substitute data collection exists**.
- It is required for implementation of numerous federal programs: FSA county committee elections and beginning-farmer loan eligibility, RMA crop insurance rating, farm bill program design and funding formulas, and rural development allocations.
- Congressional appropriators are actively defending it ($46M designated line; frequency directive in FY2026 agreement).
- Notably, the administration's own stated rationale for cutting the Farm Labor and Mink surveys was that they had "**no statutory requirement**" — logic that reinforces the census's protected position.

**Evidence for Moderate/High Risk:** None applicable — authorization is explicit and specific, and there are no alternative collections.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** This is the census's single strongest protective factor.

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- **Staffing loss exceeds the 40% threshold**: ASA's *Nation's Data at Risk 2025* estimates NASS lost **41% of staff since FY2024**; ASA's 2026 response to the USDA Data RFI puts the decline at **54% — from 839 FTE (FY2023) to 389 (FY2026)**. In May 2025 alone, 243 NASS employees (~30%) took the deferred resignation/buyout (DTN/Progressive Farmer).
- **Leadership effectively hollowed out**: as of November 2025, the associate administrator is acting; three of six units in the administrator's office have acting directors (two have no one officially in charge); four of seven divisions have acting directors, three of them double-hatted (ASA).
- **Census-specific staffing cut 57%** (230 → 100 FTE) in the FY2026 budget, and the reorganization plan consolidates NASS's 12 regional offices into 5 hubs with directed reassignments — "decline reassignment will result in termination" (USDA reorg FAQ, Oct. 2025) — likely driving further attrition of experienced field staff before the 2027 census.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The *budget* cut is modest: FY2026 request/agreement of $185M vs. $187.85M enacted ≈ **-1.5% nominal (~4% real)**, well below the 10–19% band. FY2025 was flat vs. FY2024 (≈2.4% real loss; ~14.5% purchasing-power loss since FY2009).

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** Not supportable given staffing figures.

**Finding: High Risk.** Staffing losses far exceed the 40% threshold and leadership is largely acting/vacant, even though the budget-line cut is small. This is the dataset's most severe risk category.

## Policy

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- There have been "significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities" at NASS: discontinuation of two surveys explicitly framed as efficiency/burden-reduction actions (90 FR 42560), elimination of state/regional reports, and the FY2026 budget's statement that funds were "redirected towards high-priority projects… aligned with the interests and support requirements of farmers and ranchers and the Administration."
- The 2027 census ICR was **"approved with change"** by OIRA (Sept. 16, 2026) — content changes exist but are not fully documented publicly yet.
- However: no Presidential-Action-driven ICR targets the census, no negative policy note appears on the AgCensus site, and **the census itself has not been terminated, delayed, or stripped of content**.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The pattern above shows the administration is actively reshaping NASS's portfolio and has demonstrated willingness to kill collections lacking statutory protection — the census survives precisely because of its statute. Administration officials' statements (reorganization memos, budget justifications) signal continued alignment of data programs with administration priorities, and OIRA-level content changes to the 2027 questionnaire are pending/unclear.
- The broader USDA reorganization (relocating NASS functions out of DC; building closures) is a pending structural change whose effects on the census are not yet known.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** Not supportable — notable changes affecting the publishing agency have occurred since January 2025, even if the census product itself remains intact.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** The census has not itself been targeted, but proposed/pending changes, OIRA-approved questionnaire changes, and demonstrated agency-level intervention warrant elevated caution. Preservationists should archive the 2022 census products now rather than assume continuity of access.
